name: Ivan Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a usual shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43 and have handled calls and chats here for years. I finished secondary school, know the billing routes, and do about as well as the rest of the experienced agents. I like finding the missing adjustment in a long account, though the low pay for this work makes the late shift hard to justify.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do those shifts need to support at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Salma works at the bus depot, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. Our savings would not cover a full month of expenses, and there are few other centres close by. I use AI for a draft now and then, after someone has shown me where it works, but I still check the ledger myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues a short summary is fine if the person on the call remains responsible for the bill. I would ask the team to record errors before the centre calls it a saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my experienced role would continue, but the mortgage is already close to our two wages. Salma's depot hours sometimes change, and we have less than a month saved. AI staying small does not make that safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep taking the disputed bills and check any AI draft against the ledger. I would bring a list of wrong summaries to the next staff meeting and put a little of each pay toward the mortgage reserve. In the first year, we would hold off replacing the living-room chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about money, though calm about the work itself. A broken car would eat the savings before AI even enters the conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which summary error would you put on the list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A credit that appears on the wrong month. One caller thought we still owed her money because the draft missed the date, and I had to read the ledger aloud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Salma agree to wait on the chair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. It has a torn arm, but it still holds a person. A car repair or missed depot shift costs more than an untidy room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the floor the easy billing chats might go first and ask what remains on each paid roster. I would join the union meeting to seek published hour figures and paid training for work that stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a shorter queue could mean fewer agents even if the hard calls remain. I am average at this job, not irreplaceable, and the company could put more disputes on each desk. With under a month saved and few nearby centres, lost hours would hit us quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would test the new answer tool on paid time if the company runs a trial, and log any bad billing adjustments. I would join the union meeting with our roster and ask for paid practice on the remaining complex calls. In the first year, if my hours fall I would apply for a posted paid billing vacancy nearby only if the written wage and hours cover our mortgage, keeping this wage until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious at the thought of a smaller rota. A tool that helps one person can still take away another person's shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union to request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hours by shift, the plan for junior agents and a paid place to learn the work that remains. I want the request to come from more than one worried desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a posted paid role required it and the cost left the mortgage money safe. I would ask for employer funding before using our tiny reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues AGI by 2028 puts our calls and bill checks at risk before robots arrive. I would ask the union to demand written notice and funded training for named paid posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect full thinking AI could remove most of my desk in 2028. Robots around 2031 do not buy a phone worker three more years. Salma's wage alone cannot cover our mortgage and the children, and our savings would run out fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would attend the union meeting on notice, keep our reserve for the mortgage and collect the written requirements for local paid vacancies. I would take a funded course only if a named posted job requires it and study time is paid. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, if my job ends I would apply for a paid accounts role with written wage and hours covering the mortgage; I would not leave for a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed, but I can still ask for terms and look at openings. Less than a month saved is an emergency clock, not a career break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the depot cover the mortgage for a while?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Salma could cover some food and bills, but not the whole mortgage payment. We would ask the lender about a temporary arrangement before missing one if my wage stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about a job farther away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with a signed offer whose pay covers the mortgage and longer travel. I would not move the children on a vacancy notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team five years gives time to ask which paid jobs remain and to train for them properly. I would stay active in union meetings so the hours and vacancies are recorded, not guessed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still think many calls could go by 2031, but I could learn account review if the company pays for it. We need both wages for the mortgage. I cannot leave to study full time while my family needs both wages for the mortgage. Robots in 2034 are a later change than the screen work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask to shadow account review during a paid shift and keep a record of the disputed bills I solve. I would attend union meetings about a funded course tied to a posted review job. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my calls end I would apply for that paid job only if its written wage and hours cover the mortgage; I would keep my current wage until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious but not cornered. Five years gives me time to test the work before depending on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take the review course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would complete it if the company paid for the course and my study hours, and a posted paid vacancy required it. Until then I would learn only during my regular paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say I am trying a different kind of work while keeping our home steady. I would not make them choose their future jobs around my guess about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues a decade is enough time to build a paid route into other work, if management and workers start now. I would ask the union to review the roster each year so early cuts do not hide behind a 2036 date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when AGI arrives in 2036, and the mortgage might still be ours to pay. I could become good at account review before then, but I do not assume a desk will remain after full AGI. Robots around 2039 come later than the software that changes our calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep my billing shifts and ask for one paid review session each month if the centre allows it. I would add small sums to our mortgage reserve and attend the yearly union roster meeting. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if my calls end I would apply for a posted paid account role only if the written wage and hours cover the mortgage; I would leave only after an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the end of this work and anxious about our bills now. Ten years gives me a route, but not a free month on the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the review session is not paid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would keep the current shifts and ask questions on cases I already handle. I cannot give the centre a free day each month while our reserve is thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you plan to stop work at 53?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I do not know our mortgage balance then, and I have not set an age to stop earning. I want a job whose pay actually arrives.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Our savings would not cover even a month of lost wages, and few centres are close by. Written notice, a funded course with paid time for a posted job, and an offer with mortgage-covering hours and wages would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a call is counted as solved when the customer rings again tomorrow. The ledger remembers a wrong credit even after the dashboard calls it done.

headlineQuote: The ledger remembers a wrong credit even after the dashboard calls it done.
portrait: Ivan is a **43-year-old experienced** customer service agent with secondary school education and average skill.
He earns **lower pay**, supports two school-age children and a mortgage with Salma, and has less than a month saved.
Few nearby jobs make lost **hours** a direct household threat.
He uses AI **occasionally**, checks the ledger and joins union meetings for paid routes into posted work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his calls before the family builds a mortgage reserve.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, funded paid-time training for a posted job and an offer with mortgage-covering pay would help.
